name: Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library
see: Start here. From the rooftop, the banded buttes around Medora show the yellowish Bullion Creek layers, the oldest rock exposed in the South Unit.
story: Medora sits in the valley the Little Missouri carved through these layers. Everything you will see on the Scenic Loop Drive is a chapter of the same story: swamp forests, burning coal and a river turned by glaciers.

name: Skyline Vista
see: You are standing on a gravel bench left by the Little Missouri during the Ice Age, roughly 260 feet above the river that left it.
story: The flat ground here is an old river floor. As the river cut deeper, it left benches like this one stranded high above the valley. The higher the bench, the older the gravel.

name: Scoria Point Overlook
see: Red clinker caps the ridges around you. Look for the three-part stack: yellowish Bullion Creek below, a red clinker band, gray-brown Sentinel Butte above.
story: The red rock is baked rock, not lava. A coal seam at the base of the Sentinel Butte layers burned underground and fired the clay above it like brick. Harder than its neighbors, the clinker now armors the ridgetops.

name: Wind Canyon Trail
see: Soft sandstone sculpted into pockets and fins, and a big bend of the Little Missouri below.
story: The river below is still at work. Every flood shaves a little more off the cutbank on the outside of the bend, the same process that carved the whole badlands.

name: Coal Vein Trail
see: Ground that slumped as the coal beneath it burned away, and fresh red clinker baked by the fire.
story: Lightning ignited this coal seam in 1951, and it burned for 26 years before going out in 1977. As the coal turned to ash, the ground above collapsed into the void. It is the most recent burn of the HT Butte lignite, the seam that made the South Unit's thick red clinker.

name: Buck Hill
see: One of the highest points in the South Unit, with landslides on its flanks.
story: Some of the South Unit's largest landslides surround Buck Hill. Weak clay layers soak up water and let whole hillsides slide.

name: Boicourt Overlook
see: A wide view of the eastern badlands, where two beds of petrified stumps run through the slopes.
story: Near Boicourt Spring and Badlands Overlook, geologists traced two separate stump beds, each the floor of a forest that stood here 60 million years ago.

name: Painted Canyon Visitor Center
see: The classic badlands panorama right off I-94: gray-brown Sentinel Butte layers, black coal seams and red clinker.
story: Petrified stumps still stand in their growth position in the slopes around the visitor center. Seasonal hours.

name: Petrified Forest Plateau
see: Two layers of upright petrified stumps on the west side of the plateau. A long hike from the Petrified Forest trailhead, about 50 minutes from Medora on dirt and gravel roads.
story: The park holds the third-highest concentration of petrified wood in the United States, according to the National Park Service. The trees were conifers, probably relatives of today's bald cypress and redwoods, that grew with their roots in swamp water. Floods buried their bases; the tops rotted away; silica turned the buried wood to stone. Stumps here reach about six feet tall and four feet across.
note: Pin marks the plateau, not the trailhead. Check road conditions with the park first. Collecting petrified wood in the park is illegal.

name: Slump Block Pullout
see: Giant blocks of layered rock tilted back into the hillside at 25 to 50 degrees.
story: These blocks broke loose from the valley wall and rotated as they slid. By matching the lower yellow bed in a block to the same bed in the cliff above, geologists showed one block dropped about 120 feet.
note: Approximate location, from the section cited in NDGS Misc. Series 86.

name: Cannonball Concretions Pullout
see: Round and log-shaped concretions weathering out of the basal Sentinel Butte sandstone.
story: A concretion forms when minerals cement sand grains together underground, often around a small core. The cemented ball is harder than the loose sand around it, so when erosion strips the soft sand away, the "cannonballs" are left behind.
note: Approximate location, from the section cited in NDGS Misc. Series 86.

name: Caprock Coulee Trail
see: Blue bentonite benches, hard sandstone caprocks and small slumps along the trail.
story: Caprocks are slabs of harder sandstone that shield the softer clay beneath them, leaving pillars and hoodoos as everything around them washes away.

name: Oxbow Overlook
see: The blue bentonite and white ash band, the yellow bed above it, and a huge hummocky landslide below the overlook.
story: During the Ice Age the Little Missouri flowed north toward Hudson Bay. Glaciers blocked that route, at least 640,000 years ago, and forced the river east along the edge of the ice. The new route was shorter and steeper, so the river started cutting down fast. The bend below you is the result.

name: Sperati Point
see: Old upland river gravel on the point, and granite boulders carried here by glaciers.
story: The gravel on top was dropped by rivers before the badlands were carved. South of the point, scattered granite and limestone boulders mark the southwestern edge of the ice sheets. Granite does not occur in any rock layer in the park; the glaciers brought it.

name: Elkhorn Ranch Unit
see: Roosevelt's home ranch site on a river terrace, facing the cliffs he described.
story: The ranch house stood on a low bench of river sediment above the Little Missouri. Across the river rise banded cliffs of the Bullion Creek Formation. Remote: check road conditions first.
